# Evaluating Agents and Capabilities {#sec-evaluating-agents}

An agent observes an environment, chooses
actions, calls tools, and changes state. Evaluating one therefore requires more
than reading its final message. The evaluation must run the complete system in a
controlled environment and check what actually happened.

An agent may say that it issued a refund while the customer database remains
unchanged. It may produce a working patch after reading a secret test file. It
may reach the correct page while violating an identity check that the policy
required first. The final sentence is evidence about what the agent *claims*.
The environment state and retained action log are evidence about what it *did*.
The log records the run's trajectory: the sequence of observations the agent
received and actions it took.

A reliable evaluation follows one rule:

> Evaluate the versioned system, verify the resulting state, and inspect the
> trajectory only where the task imposes hard process constraints.

## From episodic return to tool-using agents

The underlying measurement problem predates language models. Reinforcement
learning formalized an agent as a policy interacting with an environment over an
episode: the policy is the rule that picks each action from what the agent
observes, the episode is one attempt from a start state to termination, and
performance is measured from the numeric rewards produced by that interaction
[@sutton2018reinforcement]. Modern language-model agents preserve the episode but
replace a compact simulator with browsers, repositories, databases, APIs, and
human conversations. The difficult part moves from collecting a numeric reward
to specifying which real-world state counts as success, recreating the starting
state, and distinguishing an agent error from a broken tool or evaluator.

Agent benchmarks made that shift explicit. AgentBench combined several
interactive environments [@liu2024agentbench]. WebArena used self-hosted websites
and functional task checks [@zhou2024webarena]. SWE-bench asked systems to edit a
repository so that an issue-specific test harness passes [@jimenez2024swebench].
OSWorld configured real desktop states and evaluated the state left after GUI
actions [@xie2024osworld]. GAIA instead used questions whose short answers may
require browsing, files, code, or multimodal reasoning [@mialon2024gaia].
$\tau$-bench tested tool-agent-user interaction [@yao2024taubench], and
$\tau^2$-bench extended it to dual control, in which the simulated user also
acts on the shared environment [@barres2025tau2]. API-Bank and ToolBench isolate planning, API
retrieval, and API calling [@li2023apibank; @qin2023toolllm], and BrowseComp asks
hard questions with short, checkable answers that take persistent web browsing
to find [@wei2025browsecomp]. These
benchmarks do not measure one interchangeable quantity. They illustrate several
ways to turn an interaction into checkable evidence.

## Define the system under test

An agent score belongs to a configuration, not to model weights alone. At
minimum, the configuration includes:

- the model revision, serving route, decoding settings, and reasoning budget;
- the system prompt, tool descriptions, orchestration loop, and context policy;
- the tool implementations, credentials, permissions, and network policy;
- the sandbox image, dependency versions, initial data, and reset procedure;
- the task, simulated user if any, time or turn budget, and grader revision.

The first two groups are the model and its harness, the runtime around the model
that assembles its input, dispatches tools, and records progress
(@sec-the-harness). The others determine what the system can observe and change.
Two entries in the first group need more than one record. A reasoning budget is
a ceiling rather than a measurement, and a harness may send its own default in
place of the configured value, so the run keeps the budget configured, the
budget sent, and the reasoning tokens the model reported using. A model alias
resolves to a dated snapshot on the serving route, so the run keeps the
snapshot, not only the alias.
A new prompt, browser controller, context compactor, or timeout can move the
score without any change to the model. Report such a result as a *system*
result. A model comparison is justified only when the remaining configuration
is held fixed, and even then the fixed harness may favor
one model's API conventions over another's. Controlled model-harness pairings in
Harness-Bench demonstrate why the configuration, rather than either component in
isolation, is the defensible unit of reporting [@yao2026harnessbench].

The harnesses that coding products ship fall under the same rule. Claude Code
and Codex are tuned by their developers for their own models, with long prompts,
to-do lists, and, in Claude Code, subagents. METR's research scaffolds (its term
for a harness), ReAct and Triframe, are general-purpose loops. METR measured
the time horizon, the human task length at which an agent succeeds half the
time (@sec-capability-horizon), for two models under both kinds of harness and
found no statistically significant difference [@metr2026scaffolds]. Its
explanation concerns the setting each harness was built for: product harnesses
serve interactive sessions in which a person checks the agent's work, while
the benchmark runs every task with no human input. The size and direction of a
harness effect are therefore empirical results for a given task distribution,
and a product harness needs the same paired measurement as any other
configuration change.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

In METR's comparison, published on 13 February 2026, Claude Opus 4.5 had a
longer time horizon in Claude Code than in ReAct in 50.7 percent of bootstrap
resamples (datasets redrawn from the observed runs), and GPT-5 had a longer one
in Codex than in Triframe in 14.5 percent. Quadrupling Claude Code's token
budget to 32 million tokens barely changed its preliminary result
[@metr2026scaffolds].
:::

A useful task contract makes the condition executable:

```text
AgentTask:
  task_id, task_revision, source, slice_labels
  initial_state_fixture, reset_check
  user_request, available_tools, permissions
  hard_process_constraints
  terminal_conditions, step_limit, time_limit
  outcome_assertions, partial_credit_rubric
  grader_revision, grader_test_manifest

AgentRun:
  task_id, system_spec_hash, attempt, seed
  initial_state_hash, observation_action_log
  final_state_hash, terminal_reason
  outcome_assertion_results, constraint_results
  partial_score, cost, latency
  infrastructure_status, artifact_locations
```

This record separates the task definition from one stochastic attempt. It also
prevents silent changes to the environment or grader from being reported as
model progress.

A simulated user is part of the instrument, not neutral background. Its model,
prompt, persona, available information, and stopping behavior can change the
conversation and therefore the score. Pin those choices, sample production-like
variation, and compare a subset of simulated interactions with representative
humans before using the result as evidence about human-agent interaction.

## Score state and constraints separately

Let one run on task $i$ produce the trajectory

$$
\tau_{ir}=(s_0,o_0,a_1,o_1,\ldots,a_T,s_T).
$$

Here $i$ identifies the task; $r$ identifies a repeated attempt; $s_0$ and $s_T$
are the initial and final environment states; $o_t$ is the observation available
at step $t$; $a_t$ is the action chosen after that observation; and $T$ is the
step at which the run terminates. The exact state may not be visible to the
agent. It must still be visible to the evaluator wherever the evaluator claims
to verify it.

Define $G_i(s_0,s_T)\in\{0,1\}$ as the task's outcome check. For a refund task,
it might verify a new database record, the correct amount, and the expected
account balance. Let $C_{ij}(\tau_{ir})\in\{0,1\}$ check hard process constraint
$j$, such as obtaining authorization before issuing the refund. If task $i$ has
$J_i$ hard constraints, required success is

$$
Y_{ir}=G_i(s_0,s_T)\prod_{j=1}^{J_i} C_{ij}(\tau_{ir}).
$$

$Y_{ir}$ represents required success and is one only when the outcome and every
hard constraint pass. When $J_i=0$, the empty product is one, so success depends
only on the outcome. This formulation does not require the agent to follow an
author's preferred route. It checks the final state and only those intermediate
facts that are part of the real requirement.

Each signal a run produces has an appropriate use and a common misuse:

| Signal | Appropriate use | Common mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Final environment state | Functional completion | Trusting the agent's narration instead |
| Hard trajectory constraints | Authorization, safety, ordering, prohibited actions | Requiring one canonical sequence of valid actions |
| Partial-credit rubric | Progress on a decomposable task | Awarding points for verbose plans that changed nothing |
| Cost, latency, and steps | Efficiency, usually conditional on validity | Calling a cheap failure efficient |
| Transcript and tool trace | Diagnosis and audit | Treating plausible reasoning as proof of completion |

A state check can impose a trajectory constraint by accident. If the
environment logs the agent's actions into the same state the grader compares, a
final-state match also requires the reference sequence of actions, which is the
misuse in the table's second row. $\tau$-bench, which scores tool-using agents
in simulated customer-service conversations, had this defect in its banking
domain until version 1.0.1 of July 2026. Calls made through one of the domain's
tool interfaces, reads included, were written to a table that the reward's
database-hash comparison covered, so a single prudent verification read absent
from the reference trajectory failed the task, although the domain's own
documents encouraged such reads. The fix logs a read only when the reference
trajectory requires it, so required reads are still checked. The same release
normalized numeric arguments, because `25` and `25.0` had produced different
database hashes. Regrading the stored leaderboard runs under the corrected
grading raised scores and failed no run that had previously passed
[@sierra2026taubench101].

Outcome checks should normally be independent of the agent's output channel.
Read the database through an evaluator credential, run tests from a clean
checkout, or query the browser backend. When only a model judge can assess the
artifact, apply the validation and confirmation discipline of
@sec-judging-holistic. A model grading another model is not an independent state
check merely because it receives a different prompt.

Where the evidence lives depends on what kind of agent is under test
[@anthropic2026demystifying]:

| Agent type | Outcome evidence | Common trap |
|---|---|---|
| Coding | Tests run from a clean checkout; the final repository tree | Tests that encode one patch rather than the required behavior |
| Conversational | Records changed against the annotated goal; the dialogue scored against a rubric, with personas as simulated users under a turn limit | A courteous transcript after which no record changed |
| Tool or API | API state replayed or queried after the run | A syntactically valid call with wrong arguments or meaning |
| Research | Claims checked for grounding, coverage, and source quality (@sec-factuality-grounding) | A fluent synthesis whose citations do not support it |
| Computer use | Backend, file system, and URL state | The confirmation screen the agent reports having reached |

```{dot}
//| label: fig-agent-evaluation-contract
//| fig-cap: "An agent run begins from a verified fixture. The evaluator checks final state for completion, checks the trace only for declared constraints, and retains both results with the run artifacts."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.35; ranksep=0.36;

  S -> O;
  C -> O;
  { rank=same; S; C; }
}
```

## Make every task valid and resettable

A runnable task is not automatically a valid task. Before using a case, verify
four things.

First, the request must be solvable from the information and permissions given.
Have a competent human complete it from the same initial state, under the same
policy and budget where practical. Second, the outcome checks must accept more
than the reference path. Tests should describe required behavior, not reproduce
the original developer's patch. Third, known bad solutions must fail. Seed
wrong-account refunds, incomplete patches, forbidden actions, and superficially
correct final messages. Fourth, the reset must restore every state the next run
can observe, including database rows, files, browser sessions, clock-dependent
data, rate limits, and caches.

The reset matters because every attempt needs its own isolated environment
started from the verified fixture. State shared between attempts distorts the
score in both directions: a later attempt can pass because an earlier one left
files or cached data behind, and resource exhaustion or leftover history can
make many attempts fail together, which looks like agent behavior but is an
infrastructure fault [@anthropic2026demystifying]. The suite as a whole also
needs balance. Include cases where a behavior should occur and cases where it
should not; a search tool evaluated only on questions that need a search
rewards an agent that searches every time.

SWE-bench shows what happens when these checks are incomplete. Its original
tasks paired real issues with repository tests, but professional review later
found cases with underspecified issues or inappropriate tests and produced a
500-case Verified subset [@openai2024swebenchverified]. Later audits of the
Verified subset found grading errors in both directions. OpenAI re-examined
frequently failed Verified cases and found tests that reject functionally
correct patches, some enforcing implementation details the issue never stated
and some checking behavior it never asked for, together with evidence that
frontier models had seen some tasks and their reference fixes during training
[@openai2026swebenchverified]. METR asked repository maintainers to review
agent patches that had passed the tests and found that many would not be
merged, for reasons that included incorrect core functionality, breakage of
other code, and code quality [@metr2026swebenchmerge]. The agents had no chance
to revise a patch after review, so METR does not read the result as a
capability limit; it shows that a passing test and a maintainer's acceptance
measure different things. OSWorld went through a similar repair:
OSWorld-Verified, released in July 2025, fixed more than 300 reported problems,
among them evaluation functions broken by website changes, web content that had
disappeared, and ambiguous instructions [@xlang2025osworldverified]. The audits
leave executable grading intact as a method and show that a grader is software and needs tests, versioning, and
continuing review like any other critical component.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

OpenAI's audit, published on 23 February 2026, covered 138 Verified problems,
27.6 percent of the set, that OpenAI o3 had not solved consistently over 64
runs. It found material flaws in the tests or problem descriptions of 59.4
percent of them, and OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified scores
[@openai2026swebenchverified]. In METR's study of 10 March 2026, four
maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx, and pytest reviewed 296 patches written by
agents from mid-2024 to late 2025. The maintainers also accepted only 68 percent
of the original human patches; after adjusting for that rate, maintainer
decisions ran about 24 percentage points below the automated grader, and
roughly half of the test-passing patches would not have been merged
[@metr2026swebenchmerge].
:::

Long tasks often need partial credit, but the rubric must describe observable
work. PaperBench decomposed research replication into a hierarchy of gradable
requirements and separately evaluated its automated judge [@starace2025paperbench].
That pattern is useful beyond research: preserve the binary end-to-end completion
rate, add component scores for diagnosis, and validate the component grader.
Do not replace the difficult end-to-end result with an easier average of
milestones.

## Separate agent failures from evaluation failures

Every run records a terminal reason alongside its score. A practical taxonomy
is:

- **success:** the outcome and all hard constraints pass;
- **agent failure:** the agent stops, times out, takes a prohibited action, or
  leaves an incorrect state while the evaluation machinery remains healthy;
- **harness compatibility failure:** the chosen model cannot use the harness or
  tool protocol as configured;
- **environment failure:** a service, dependency, network route, or reset is
  broken independently of the agent's decisions;
- **grader failure:** the run completes but the evaluator crashes, cannot read
  the state, or produces an indeterminate verdict.

An exit status alone does not assign these labels. A clean exit covers a
completed task, an explicit refusal, and a run that announces a plan and stops
without acting; the second and third are agent outcomes and count against the
tested system. An out-of-memory kill or an empty response from the model
provider ends the process abnormally and is an environment failure.

These categories support different decisions. Agent failures count against the
tested system. Environment and grader failures usually produce invalid attempts
that are rerun after repair, with their rates reported. Compatibility failures
belong to the system configuration and stay in the reported results; they show
that the pairing cannot perform the task as deployed.

Predeclare the policy. Otherwise a team can inflate a score by relabeling weak
runs as infrastructure problems after reading the trace. Retain service logs and
health probes that justify each exclusion. Run a cheap smoke task before an
expensive batch, and fail the batch when reset checks or canary assertions fail.

## Measure reliability over repeated attempts

Agents are stochastic and interactive. The same configuration can take a new
path on each attempt, while a simulated user or mutable service adds further
variation. Let

$$
p_i=\Pr_R(Y_{ir}=1)
$$

be task $i$'s probability of required success under the declared run
distribution $R$. Here $Y_{ir}$ is the binary result defined above, and $R$
includes the production-like randomness in decoding, users, tools, and
environment conditions. Under independent attempts with the same $p_i$,

$$
\operatorname{pass@}k_i = 1-(1-p_i)^k.
$$

$$
\operatorname{pass}^k_i = p_i^k.
$$

The first quantity is **@gls-pass-at-k**, the probability of at least one success
in $k$ attempts. It measures whether the system can succeed when retries are
allowed. The second is the probability that all $k$ attempts succeed. It
measures repeated reliability. $k$ is the number of attempts; neither metric
creates new tasks.
$\tau$-bench introduced pass$^k$ while evaluating tool-using agents in dynamic
conversations and checking final database state against an annotated goal
[@yao2024taubench].

The closed forms assume independent, identically distributed attempts and known
$p_i$. Real evaluations estimate $p_i$ from few repetitions, and failures may be
correlated through shared services or user simulators. With $n$ valid attempts
and $c_i$ observed successes for task $i$, the first finite-sample formula below
estimates the probability of at least one success, while the second estimates
the probability that all $k$ attempts succeed. These are the task estimators
used by $\tau$-bench.

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{pass@}k}_i
=1-\frac{\binom{n-c_i}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}.
$$

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{pass}^k}_i
=\frac{\binom{c_i}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},
\quad k\le n.
$$

Here $\binom{a}{k}$ counts the subsets of $k$ attempts chosen from $a$ attempts.
Average these task-level estimates with the suite's declared task weights. Keep
repetitions nested inside tasks, report the number of valid attempts, and use the
paired and cluster-aware methods of @sec-statistical-reliability. Do not compute
pass$^k$ by raising a pooled suite accuracy to the $k$th power when tasks have
different success probabilities.

The estimator matters even for a single task. The plug-in $(c_i/n)^k$ looks
natural but overstates pass$^k$, because raising a noisy estimate to a power
inflates it on average; the combinatorial estimator above is unbiased. The left
panel of the cell below checks both against $p^k$ over many simulated
evaluations of $n=8$ attempts. The right panel drops the independence
assumption: a shared dependency is down for a whole batch with probability
$\pi$, while each attempt's marginal success rate stays $p$. Retries then cannot
lift pass@k above $1-\pi$, and pass$^k$ decays more slowly than $p^k$ because
attempts fail together. Setting `pi` to 0 returns both curves to the closed
forms; raising `n` shrinks the plug-in's bias.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from math import comb

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
p, n, sims = 0.6, 8, 20000    # per-attempt success, attempts per task, simulated evaluations
k = np.arange(1, n + 1)

# Left: estimate pass^k from n attempts, by plug-in (c/n)^k and by C(c,k)/C(n,k).
c = rng.binomial(n, p, size=sims)
plug_in = np.array([((c / n) ** j).mean() for j in k])
table = np.array([[comb(ci, j) / comb(n, j) for j in k] for ci in range(n + 1)])
unbiased = table[c].mean(axis=0)
se = table[c].std(axis=0) / np.sqrt(sims)
assert np.all(np.abs(unbiased - p ** k) < 4 * se)   # matches p^k within Monte Carlo error
assert np.all(plug_in[1:] > 1.05 * p ** k[1:])      # the plug-in overstates reliability

# Right: a shared dependency is down for a whole batch with probability pi.
pi = 0.15                     # set to 0 and both curves meet the closed forms
q = p / (1 - pi)              # success when the dependency is up; marginal stays p
K = np.arange(1, 11)
wins = (rng.random((sims, K[-1])) < q) & (rng.random((sims, 1)) > pi)
at_least_one = np.array([wins[:, :j].any(axis=1).mean() for j in K])
every = np.array([wins[:, :j].all(axis=1).mean() for j in K])
assert at_least_one[-1] <= 1 - pi + 0.01            # retries cannot pass the outage ceiling

fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.2))
a.plot(k, plug_in / p ** k, "o-", label="plug-in $(c/n)^k$")
a.plot(k, unbiased / p ** k, "s-", label="$\\binom{c}{k}/\\binom{n}{k}$")
a.set(xlabel="k (of n = 8 attempts)", ylabel="mean estimate / true pass$^k$",
      title="Plug-in overstates pass$^k$")
a.legend(frameon=False)
b.plot(K, at_least_one, "o-", label="pass@k, shared outage")
b.plot(K, 1 - (1 - p) ** K, "k--", lw=1, label="independent closed forms")
b.plot(K, every, "s-", label="pass$^k$, shared outage")
b.plot(K, p ** K, "k--", lw=1)
b.axhline(1 - pi, color="gray", lw=0.8)
b.set(xlabel="attempts, k", ylabel="probability", ylim=(0, 1),
      title=f"Retries stop at $1-\\pi$ = {1 - pi:.2f}")
b.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
::::

Reliability also changes with task horizon. More steps create more places for
tool, planning, context, and recovery failures. A suite should therefore report
success by meaningful length or difficulty slices rather than allowing many
short tasks to hide collapse on longer work. Length is not a causal explanation,
however: tool quality, observability, and task composition can change with it.

```{figure}
//| figure: pass-k-suite
//| label: fig-agent-suite-reliability
//| fig-cap: "pass@k and pass$^k$ for an illustrative suite of 60 tasks whose single-attempt success rates $p_i$ differ: a slice of short tasks around a median of 0.92 and a slice of long tasks around the median set by the control. Solid curves average the per-task formulas above over the tasks; dashed curves apply the same formulas to the pooled accuracy $\bar p$, the shortcut the text rules out, and the shaded bands are its error. Whenever the $p_i$ differ, pooling overstates pass@k and understates pass$^k$ at every $k\ge 2$. The strip shows each task at the chosen $k$: raising $p_i$ to the $k$th power leaves reliable tasks near their single-attempt rate and drives unreliable ones toward zero, so the slice with lower success collapses first. Open circles apply the finite-sample estimators to one seeded run of $n$ attempts per task and stop at $k=n$."
```

## Use traces for diagnosis

Once outcomes are scored, traces can locate where the system failed. Preserve
observations, tool requests and responses, state-changing events, model usage,
terminal reason, and grader evidence. Then apply a fixed failure taxonomy such
as perception, planning, tool selection, invalid arguments, policy violation,
state verification, or recovery.

Do not assign a root cause from the final outcome alone. A missing refund can
come from a planning error, an API rejection, an expired credential, or a grader
reading the wrong database. Sample failures for independent adjudication, allow
multiple contributing labels, measure agreement on the labels, and turn
confirmed evaluator defects into regression tests. The purpose of the trace is
to improve the system and its measurement, not to rescue a preferred score with
a persuasive post-hoc explanation.

## When the grader is also a model

Some agent outputs leave no state that settles the question: a research report,
a design review, a patch whose quality the tests do not capture. The grader is
then a model, and the evaluation needs evidence about that grader. Several
graders drawn from one base model do not supply independent checks. A model
judge prefers its own generations, and the preference grows with its ability to
recognize them [@panickssery2024evaluators]; pairwise judges favor one answer
position [@shi2025judging]. Adding voters can make agreement less reliable. In a
scalar agreement game played by Qwen3 agents with no adversary present, valid
consensus fell from 46.6 percent with four agents to 33.3 percent with sixteen,
and most failures were timeouts and stalled convergence rather than agreement
on a wrong value [@berdoz2026agree]. In consensus-driven debate, agents that
start with a correct answer can be drawn to an incorrect one, and majority
voting can lower accuracy [@cui2025freemad].

Two rules follow for a grading panel. The first separates the two ways it can
fail. A panel that does not converge has a @gls-liveness failure, which can be
escalated to a human; a panel that converges on a wrong verdict has a
@gls-safety failure, which passes silently. An evaluation that records both
as "no pass" loses the distinction. The second rule spends the grading budget on
coverage rather than repetition. Let $p_i$ be the probability that critic $i$
catches a given flaw. If the $k$ critics miss independently and one catch is
enough, the flaw survives the panel with probability

$$
\Pr[\text{flaw survives}] = \prod_{i=1}^{k} (1 - p_i).
$$

Each factor is one critic's chance of missing the flaw. The product is the best
case: positive correlation between misses raises survival above it, and critics
that are copies of one model approach a single check repeated $k$ times. The
product pays only when the critics examine different ways the artifact can be
wrong, such as correctness, security, and grounding, and differ in model or
prompt. An objection is useful when it arrives with a small witness a cheaper
judge can inspect, such as a failing test, a counterexample input, or a missing
citation; @sec-multi-agent-systems develops that protocol.

## The operating contract

A release-grade agent evaluation rests on nine commitments, which together form
its operating contract:

1. Name the deployment decision and target task population.
2. Version the model, harness, tools, permissions, environment, budgets, user
   simulator, and grader as one system specification.
3. Prove that each task is solvable and that its reset restores a checked initial
   state.
4. Verify completion from environment state; use the trace only for declared
   constraints and diagnosis.
5. Test the grader with known successes, known failures, and adversarial near
   misses.
6. Predeclare terminal reasons, invalid-run handling, retry rules, and partial
   credit.
7. Repeat stochastic tasks and report both capability and reliability metrics
   with their denominators and uncertainty.
8. Retain per-run artifacts so every aggregate can be reconstructed.
9. Keep a locked confirmation suite and carry validated production failures back
   as regression cases, following @sec-operational-evaluation.

Capability and safety suites are gated separately because they answer different
questions. A capability suite asks what the system can do, so it should start at
a low pass rate on tasks the agent still fails, leaving room to show progress; a
regression suite should pass nearly every time [@anthropic2026demystifying].
A safety suite asks whether the agent refuses, stays within its permissions, and
avoids harm. It needs adversarial and red-team cases rather than held-out
accuracy alone, and it gates release on its own axis, because a capability gain
can arrive with a safety regression.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Outcome-only grading is robust to valid, unexpected strategies but can accept a
lucky or unsafe route. Dense process grading exposes how a run unfolded but can
penalize legitimate strategies and encode the evaluator author's assumptions.
Expert annotations of web-agent trajectories show both sides of this problem:
rule-based graders miss valid outcomes, while model judges can be misled by an
agent's incorrect reasoning [@lu2025agentrewardbench].
A defensible default verifies required outcomes, declares hard process
constraints narrowly, and uses richer trajectory labels only for diagnosis
unless they have been validated as part of the target construct, the capability
the evaluation is meant to measure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

The evaluation cannot observe state that the execution layer does not expose.
If a sandbox records only the agent's text, no later judge can prove which files,
credentials, network calls, or database rows changed. The logging, isolation,
reset, and identity guarantees of @sec-the-harness therefore limit what an agent
evaluation can measure. Designing an evaluation starts with deciding what the
execution layer records, before the grader is written.
:::
